title: Peak of Every Window
statement:
Given an array of integers nums and a window size k, slide a window of exactly k consecutive elements from the left end of the array to the right end, one step at a time.

Return an array with the largest value in each window, in order from the leftmost window to the rightmost. There are nums.length − k + 1 windows.

examples.why: When 12 leaves, the next peak is 8, an older value, not 5, the newest one. You need to remember more than the current maximum.
Falling values: each window's peak is its older element, which leaves right after.
With k = 1 every element is its own window. Starting a running maximum at 0 would give wrong answers for negatives.

hints: Recomputing the max of each window costs O(k) per window. When the current max leaves, what do you need to know?
If a newer value is at least as big as an older one, can the older one ever be the peak of a later window?
Keep a deque of indexes whose values decrease from front to back. A new value removes every smaller-or-equal value from the back. The front is the peak; drop it when it slides out of the window.

explain.intuition:
Suppose an older value a sits in the window and a newer value b ≥ a arrives. Every future window that still contains a also contains b, and b stays longer. So a can never be a peak again; you can forget it now.

After forgetting all such values, the survivors decrease from oldest to newest. That list lives in a deque of indexes: new values join at the back after evicting smaller ones, the peak is at the front, and the front leaves when its index falls out of the window. Each index enters once and leaves once, so the whole pass is O(n). It is the same idea as a "next greater element" stack, with a second exit at the front.
steps: Keep a deque of indexes. For each i:
If the front index is ≤ i − k, it has left the window: remove it.
While the value at the back is ≤ nums[i], remove it from the back. Then push i.
Once i ≥ k − 1, the window is full: append nums[front] to the answer.
pitfalls: Keeping only the current maximum. When it leaves, you have no idea what the next one is, as in the first example.
Using Array.prototype.shift for the front in JavaScript. It is O(n) per call on large arrays. Keep a head index instead.
Storing values instead of indexes in the deque. You then cannot tell when the front has slid out of the window.

solutions.title: Scan every window
solutions.idea: For each window, find its maximum directly.

solutions.title: Monotonic deque of indexes
solutions.idea: Keep only the values that could still become a peak. They decrease from front to back, so the front is always the answer.

followups: Return the minimum of every window instead. What single change does the deque need?
Solve it with a max-heap of (value, index) pairs. What is the complexity, and why is it worse?
